caption.before: Pick a shown two-action game and shrink the common epsilon (log scale). This illustration uses the **uniform family**, confining each player's first-action probability to $[\varepsilon,1-\varepsilon]$. The blue and orange steps are best-reply correspondences within that square, and green dots are its equilibria. The right panel samples these equilibria for epsilon from0.001 to0.5, with p in blue and q in orange; it does not compute a limit at zero. Rings mark Nash equilibria of the unperturbed game: green means within Euclidean distance0.004 of an equilibrium sampled at epsilon0.001; red means outside that finite threshold. Neither verdict proves a limiting classification. Full perfection allows general action-specific lower bounds as in the definition; a particular uniform family need not reach every perfect equilibrium.
caption.after: Pick a shown two-action game and shrink the common epsilon (log scale). This illustration uses the **uniform family**, confining each player's first-action probability to $[\varepsilon,1-\varepsilon]$. The blue and orange steps are best-reply correspondences within that square, and green dots are its equilibria. The right panel samples these equilibria for epsilon from 0.001 to 0.5, with p in blue and q in orange; it does not compute a limit at zero. Rings mark Nash equilibria of the unperturbed game: green means at Euclidean distance strictly less than 0.004 of an equilibrium sampled at epsilon 0.001; red means at or beyond that finite threshold. Neither verdict proves a limiting classification. Full perfection allows general action-specific lower bounds as in the definition; a particular uniform family need not reach every perfect equilibrium.
